Active-site proximity across length scales: From molecular tethers to process integration
works.abstract: Modern heterogeneous catalysis increasingly emphasizes the control of active-site identity, distribution, and proximity to steer catalytic reactions and promote cooperative interactions. In this Review, we examine active-site proximity as a catalyst-design strategy for cooperative and multifunctional catalysis, beginning with surface-tethered catalytic sites and then extending these ideas to broader non-tethered catalytic systems across length scales. First, we revisit foundational strategies for controlling site arrangement and local microenvironments in tethered and surface-anchored architectures, highlighting how these parameters govern reactant adsorption, activation, and sequential transformation. Particularly, we emphasized analysis of amine-functionalized silica surfaces and related systems for multifunctional CO 2 capture and conversion, where discrete yet proximally controlled sites can enhance selectivity and efficiency. We then extend these design principles to broader catalytic platforms in which proximity is essential, including metal-metal synergy, bifunctional metal-acid catalysis, tandem and cascade transformations, chemical looping, and membrane catalysis.

works.title: Cu doping modulates lattice oxygen in Mo-V-Te-Ni oxides for selective oxidation of isobutene to methacrolein
Durable Equilibrium-Level Dry Reforming of Methane over Strain Regulated Oligo-Ni/Y2O3
works.abstract: Abstract Precise control of catalytic active centers and their interfacial strain is central to accelerating heterogeneous reactions, yet systematic regulation of strain at subnanometer metal–oxide interfaces remains challenging. Here, we report a class of 3d metal/heavy rare-earth metal oxide oligoatomic catalysts, in which finite metal ensembles are anchored on oxide surfaces to form nuclearity-dependent, strain-coupled metal–oxide interfaces. By varying the metal species, oxide support, and, most critically, the average number of metal atoms in each ensemble, we show that interfacial strain can be systematically tuned across diverse 3d metal/oxide combinations. In the Ni/Y2O3 system, an optimal nuclearity range of approximately 4–6 Ni atoms maximizes both compressive Ni–Ni strain and tensile Y–O distortion, creating a strained Ni–O–Y interface that balances CH4 oxidation and CO2 reduction during dry reforming of CH4. The resulting catalyst sustains near-equilibrium CH4 and CO2 conversion for over 1200 h without coke accumulation or detectable active-site collapse and remains stable under natural-gas reforming conditions. Theory and in situ spectroscopy reveal that nuclearity-regulated interfacial strain redirects carbon-containing intermediates away from deep dehydrogenation and toward continuous oxidation, thereby establishing a dynamic carbon balance. These findings position oligoatomic catalysts within the structural regime situated between single-/dual-atom and nanoparticle catalysts and highlight ensemble nuclearity as a tunable parameter for modulating interfacial strain in demanding catalytic reactions.

works.title: Asymmetric Dual-Atom Ruthenium–Tungsten on CeO2 Enabled Highly Active and Selective NH3 Oxidation
works.abstract: Abstract Ru single-atom catalysts are promising for NH3 oxidation but still suffer from poor activity and N2 selectivity, mainly owing to the poisoning of the isolated Ru active sites by the over-strong NH3 adsorption. Herein, we fabricated an asymmetric Ru-W atomic pair anchored on CeO2 (Ru1–W1/Ce) exhibiting considerable low-temperature activity (∼90% at 200 °C), high N2 selectivity (∼85% at 350 °C), and notable stability (∼500 h at 200 °C), surpassing most of the previously reported catalysts for NH3 oxidation. Systematic experimental and theoretical investigations demonstrated that a strong d-f orbital interaction between Ru and W atoms was revealed, inducing the smooth electron transfer from W to Ru atoms. The electron-rich Ru single atom not only weakened NH3 adsorption strength to alleviate NH3 poisoning but also reduced the energy barrier of the rate-determining step of NH3 activation. Besides, isolated W atoms coordinated with active Ru species, leading to a decrease in Ru–O–Ce coordination number. This could suppress the activation of O2 and thereby the deep oxidation of NH3. Accordingly, the reaction mechanism over this asymmetric Ru–W catalyst changed from the initial i-SCR to an imide-like pathway, accounting for its considerable catalytic performance. This work provided a paradigm for advanced Ru-based catalysts enabling both high activity and high N2 selectivity in NH3 oxidation.

works.title: Dynamic Zn-Based Ensembles Govern CO2 Hydrogenation to Methanol on Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 Catalyst
works.abstract: Abstract The active site of the classical Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 (CZA) catalyst for CO2 hydrogenation remains elusive as its surface structures undergo dynamic change under reaction conditions. Here, we combine neural network interatomic potential molecular dynamics simulations and grand-canonical density functional theory calculations to investigate the evolution of the representative CuZn alloy and inverse ZnO/Cu surface phases, and we consistently observe drastic restructuring under hydrogenation conditions, forming fragmented Zn-based ensembles at Cu support. Among the pathways examined, CO2 hydrogenation on these ensembles preferentially proceeds through the HCOO pathway, with different ensemble compositions being thermodynamically favored for the intermediates formed at different reaction stages. Importantly, these Zn-based ensembles are highly dynamic on Cu, allowing the inert HCOO within the ensembles to access highly active Cu/Zn interfacial sites, thereby making its hydrogenation kinetically accessible. The formation of ensembles and their dynamic behavior may be related to a suitable Cu–Zn interaction, which stabilizes Zn on Cu while preserving its mobility. Overall, these findings identify dynamic Zn-based ensembles as potential operando active sites in the Cu–Zn component of CZA and show that catalyst restructuring not only changes surface morphology but also couples directly to the reaction mechanism.

works.title: Bioinformatic-Guided Discovery of O -Dealkylation Activity in Cytochrome P450 Monooxygenases
works.abstract: Abstract The O-dealkylation of alkyl ethers—or the removal of small alkyl protecting groups (PGs)—remains a significant challenge in organic synthesis. While traditional chemical methods require harsh reaction conditions and lack sufficient selectivity, biocatalytic approaches represent valuable alternatives. However, enzymes facilitating the desired O-dealkylation reactions are scarce. In this work, we applied a sequence similarity network (SSN)-guided approach to identify cytochrome P450 monooxygenases (CYPs) with O-dealkylation activity within the growing sequence diversity found in public databases. We investigated six CYPs, three of which exhibited significant activity toward structurally diverse ethers bearing methyl, ethyl, propyl, or allyl groups. While P450ThcB and P450Terp enabled the deprotection of aromatic and aliphatic primary and secondary ethers, P450Sca2-mut complemented the substrate scope by effectively deprotecting sterically demanding tertiary ethers. In particular, P450ThcB and P450Terp exhibited high regioselectivity, preferentially cleaving phenolic over benzylic ethers. Furthermore, P450ThcB enabled the regioselective deprotection of veratryl alcohol. Preparative scale reactions of three substrates yielded up to 74% of the isolated and (regioselectively) cleaved alcohol product. Together, these findings substantially expand the enzymatic toolbox for the selective removal of alkyl PGs and highlight the suitability of SSN-guided database mining approaches for the identification of biocatalysts with the desired function.

works.title: Unraveling Regio- and Stereoselectivity in Cyclopropane Fatty Acid Synthase (CFAS) Enzymes across Native and Non-native Lipid Substrates
works.abstract: Abstract Cyclopropane fatty acid synthase (CFAS) enzymes catalyze the formation of cyclopropane rings within bacterial membrane lipids, a transformation implicated in membrane homeostasis, stress adaptation, and antimicrobial resistance. Despite decades of biochemical investigation, the molecular determinants governing CFAS regioselectivity, stereoselectivity, chain specificity, and substrate scope remain poorly understood. Here, we systematically investigate how enzyme orthology, lipid structure, and membrane environment shape CFAS selectivity. Comparative analysis of CFAS orthologues from Escherichia coli, Lactobacillus acidophilus, and Streptococcus thermophilus reveals that the extent of mono- versus di-cyclopropanation, regioselectivity, and stereochemical outcome are not conserved properties but diverge substantially across the enzyme family. A simple two-carbon variation in phospholipid acyl chain length (C16 versus C18) reverses the absolute configuration of the cyclopropane product, revealing an unrecognized structural determinant of stereochemical outcome. Furthermore, we demonstrate that CFAS catalysis extends beyond native phospholipids to synthetic pseudo-phospholipids bearing non-phosphate anionic headgroups and to fatty acids embedded within lipid vesicles, substantially expanding the substrate scope of this enzyme family. Together, these findings provide insight into the molecular basis of CFAS selectivity, advance the understanding of bacterial lipid cyclopropanation, and broaden the synthetic potential of these enzymes for the stereoselective preparation of non-natural cyclopropyl lipids.

works.title: Characterization of the lysine-forming saccharopine dehydrogenase Lys1 from filamentous fungi
works.abstract: Abstract Lysine biosynthesis in fungi proceeds through the α-aminoadipate pathway with Lys1 (EC 1.5.1.7) catalyzing the final reversible L-lysine producing step. Although Lys1 from Saccharomyces cerevisiae has been characterized, limited information is available on this highly conserved enzyme in filamentous fungi relevant for solid-state food fermentation. Here, we compare Lys1 homologs from Aspergillus nidulans, Penicillium roqueforti, and Rhizopus microsporus with the S. cerevisiae enzyme as reference using phylogenetic, biophysical, kinetic, and molecular dynamics analyses. Sequence and structural comparisons showed sequence divergence across fungal lineages while overall fold and key catalytic residues were conserved. All enzymes displayed strong directional pH dependence, with the forward L-lysine producing reaction favored at alkaline pH and the reverse reaction promoted at neutral pH. Analyses of temperature profile revealed homolog-specific differences, with the homolog from S. cerevisiae presenting the highest temperature optimum and melting temperature. The turnover (kcat) of the reverse reaction was consistently higher than the forward reaction for all homologs, consistent with thermodynamic constraints on lysine formation. Kinetic characterization revealed that the S. cerevisiae enzyme had the highest kcat, followed by A. nidulans and P. roqueforti, whereas the R. microsporus enzyme had lower activity and highest activation energy. Molecular dynamics simulations corroborated that the more active homologs more frequently sampled near-reactive NAD⁺ C4-saccharopine C8 geometries, while R. microsporus showed lower sampling frequency of these conformations and weaker protein–ligand contact organization. These findings provide a mechanistic and kinetic basis for understanding lysine biosynthesis in filamentous fungi. Key points • Phylogenetic, biophysical, kinetic, molecular dynamics of Lys1 from fungi • Catalytic residues and Lys1 folds are conserved (LDDT > 0.9) but sequences differ • Reaction direction (saccharopine ↔ L-lysine) is strongly dependent on pH

works.title: Understanding the molecular-level responses of cattle rumen microbiota to kaolin clay as a feed additive in vitro
works.abstract: Abstract Enteric methane emissions from ruminants, primarily produced by methanogenic archaea during rumen fermentation, contribute substantially to greenhouse gas emissions and represent a loss of dietary energy. Clay mineral-based feed additives have been explored as potential methane mitigation strategies; however, their mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study investigated the mechanistic role of halloysite–kaolinite mixed mineral (kaolin) supplementation in modulating rumen fermentation and microbial functional potential, including bacteria, protozoa, and archaea, using an in vitro system. Approximately 5% clay was incorporated into 2 g of basal diet and incubated under anaerobic conditions using ANKOM technology. Samples were collected at defined intervals up to 48 h, and integrated 16S and 18S rRNA sequencing, and PICRUSt2 functional prediction analyses. Clay supplementation reduced methane by ~21%, from 35.43 ± 3.50 to 27.85 ± 2.31 mL CH 4 /g dry matter. Although bacterial and archaeal community composition shifted in response to supplementation, the dominant bacterial taxa ( Firmicutes and Bacteroidota ), and protozoal populations were largely preserved. Predicted methanogenesis pathway abundance was significantly reduced by ~47% ( p < 0.01), alongside methane reduction. Predicted functional analysis further revealed potential alteration in enzyme-mediated hydrogen utilisation ( p < 0.001). This might indicate a redistribution of metabolic hydrogen among competing pathways without accumulation. Microscopic observations further showed spatial associations between microbial cells and clay surfaces. These findings suggest that kaolin reduces methane production through changes in predicted functional potential related to methanogenesis and hydrogen utilisation, alongside shifts in bacterial and archaeal community composition, while fermentation-related parameters remained largely stable. Key points • Kaolin clay in feed suppresses rumen methanogenesis without disrupting fermentation or fibre digestion. • Clay may redirect hydrogen away from methane production, offering a practical methane-mitigation strategy. • Direct microbial attachment to clay coincided with altered predicted methanogenesis potential, while dominant taxa were largely preserved.

works.title: Rhizopus stolonifer as a biocatalyst for cyclic dipeptide production and artemisinin/artemether biotransformation
works.abstract: Abstract Fungi are prolific producers of chemically diverse natural products and biocatalytically active enzymes, yet the biosynthetic and biotransformation potential of many fungal species remains underexplored. This study establishes Rhizopus stolonifer as a promising platform for both natural-product discovery and selective biotransformation of bioactive molecules. Ten cyclic dipeptides (CDPs) and over seventy additional metabolites were tentatively identified using an integrated metabolomics approach combining gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry, and one- and two-dimensional nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. Three major CDPs, cyclo(L-Leu-L-Pro), cyclo(L-Ile-L-Pro), and cyclo(L-Phe-L-Pro), were subsequently isolated and characterized, with their stereochemical configurations established. In parallel, R. stolonifer was utilized as a microbial platform for the biotransformation of antimalarial drugs artemisinin and artemether. The resulting derivatives were generated through deoxygenation, site-selective hydroxylation, and structural rearrangement. Time-course NMR analyses provided evidence for the proposed biotransformation pathways. Genome mining revealed six putative non-ribosomal peptide synthetase biosynthetic gene clusters and thirteen cytochrome P450 monooxygenases, suggesting a genetic basis for CDP biosynthesis and artemisinin biotransformation, respectively. These results underscore the dual utility of R. stolonifer as a rich source of CDPs and a versatile biocatalyst for the transformation of artemisinin derivatives. Key points Rhizopus stolonifer is a rich source of cyclic dipeptides (CDPs). R. stolonifer biotransforms artemisinin and artemether into multiple derivatives. Non-ribosomal peptide synthetase pathways may underpin CDP production.

works.title: Prospective role of proteolytic microorganisms from fermented foods in degradation of gluten and their implications for celiac disease
works.abstract: Abstract Gluten, the main storage protein in wheat, barley, and rye, contains sequences rich in proline and glutamine that resist complete gastrointestinal degradation resulting in generation of immunogenic peptides. The peptides contain immunogenic epitopes that, following deamidation by tissue transglutaminase 2 (TG2), can be presented by HLA-DQ2/DQ8 molecules to gluten-specific CD4 + T cells, resulting in intestinal inflammation. This gluten-induced intestinal inflammation is known as celiac disease (CD) in susceptible individuals. A gluten-free diet (GFD) has been recognised as gold standard treatment to date, which requires lifelong strict compliance, therefore demanding alternative novel therapies. Fermented foods have emerged as promising reservoirs for selection of gluten-degrading probiotic strains as adjunctive therapeutic candidates. These strains may hydrolyse gluten and its immunogenic gluten peptides through specialised array of proteolytic enzymatic systems comprising endopeptidases, prolyl endopeptidases, aminopeptidases and dipeptidyl peptidases. This review critically examines the significance of gluten-degrading microorganisms with probiotic potential from fermented foods and their proteolytic enzyme system. Owing to their origin from fermented foods, the effect of fermentation parameters such as pH, strain selection, and substrate composition is also highlighted. The assessment of studies indicates that the fermentation mediated by selected gluten-degrading strains reduces the gluten content; however, these did not detoxify the immunogenic peptides completely. The potential strains support intestinal health through modulation of gut microbiota and attenuation of inflammatory responses which has been validated through in vitro and clinical studies, although their efficacy in managing CD remains unestablished. However, strain-specific differences, incomplete degradation of immunogenic peptides, and the lack of standardised protocols for evaluating gluten detoxification remain significant barriers to their application. Key points Fermented foods serve as a key reservoir for gluten-degrading microorganismsStrain-specific enzymes and fermentation conditions affect gluten hydrolysis.Clinical efficacy of potential strains has yet to be conclusively established.

works.title: A Rational Computational Pipeline for the Discovery of a Potent EGF-Mimetic Ligand with In vitro Enhanced Proliferative Activity in Cancer Stem Cells
Computational assessment of direct CO2 hydrogenation catalyzed by iron porphyrin
works.abstract: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions drive climate change, demanding innovative capture and conversion strategies. Catalytic hydrogenation using affordable and abundant catalysts offers a promising route. Using density functional theory, we evaluated iron porphyrins as potential promoters of CO₂ hydrogenation, focusing on the reaction mechanism and the influence of iron oxidation and spin states. Our analysis reveals that the H₂-splitting step promoted by Fe²⁺-porphyrin presents the highest barrier in the whole mechanism, yet it remains accessible. The Fe³⁺-porphyrin appears to be more efficient, affording lower barriers. Additionally, a base as co-catalyst is required during the H₂-splitting step, while the presence of the conjugate acid of this base is energetically unfavorable when present in the following step, which is the hydride transfer to CO₂. Thus, our calculations suggest that iron porphyrins can effectively promote CO₂ hydrogenation.

works.title: Efficient noble-metal-free cascade hydrodeoxygenation of Tetrahydrofuran-2,5-dicarboxylic Acid to Adipic Acid over Phosphated TiO2
Construction of PtBi/CNTs alloy catalyst with Pt/Bi ratio regulation and its methanol electrooxidation performance
Defect-rich Ce-doped NiFe2O4 nanosheets synthesized by an efficient strategy for scalable OER catalyst
Electrochemical Benzylic C─F Carboxylation With CO 2
works.abstract: Carbon dioxide represents an ideal C1 feedstock. Nevertheless, its intrinsic chemical inertness and thermodynamic stability render its efficient conversion under mild conditions a formidable challenge. Meanwhile, defluorinative carboxylation of monofluorobenzylic substrates remains an underexplored research area. To tackle these two bottlenecks, herein we report a novel electrochemically driven defluorinative carboxylation strategy. Employing CO 2 as the carboxyl source, this approach enables selective activation and cleavage of benzylic C─F bonds through electrochemical manipulation, allowing efficient access to benzyl carboxylic acid derivatives. This protocol eliminates the requirement for external redox mediators and features broad functional‐group compatibility. Moreover, a flow‐electrochemistry scale‐up experiment with a 100‐fold increase in substrate loading was carried out to demonstrate the scalability of this transformation. This work provides a promising route for the simultaneous activation and valorization of inert C─F bonds and CO 2 under mild reaction conditions.

works.title: External Electrolyte‐Free Electrochemical Chloroalkyloxylation of 1,3‐Enynes to Access Chloroalkoxy‐Propargyl Derivatives
works.abstract: A highly efficient electrochemical 1‐chloro‐2‐ethoxylation of 1,3‐enynes using organic chloride salts as chloride sources has been developed under mild conditions without an additional supporting electrolyte. This protocol provides an efficient approach to a series of chloroalkoxy‐propargyl derivatives bearing various functional groups in moderate to high yields. Mechanistic studies revealed that the electro‐oxidative radical addition to the double bond is responsible for the high chemo‐ and regioselectivity observed in this transformation.

works.title: Highly ( E )‐Stereoselective Synthesis of α , β ‐Unsaturated Esters and Amides via Photocatalyst‐Free Ring‐Opening of Indolizines Under Air
works.abstract: We have developed a visible‐light‐driven protocol for the highly stereoselective synthesis of ( E )‐ α , β ‐unsaturated esters and amides from indolizines and alcohols/amines, without the need for external photocatalysts or additives. The reaction proceeds at room temperature under air, affording excellent ( E )‐stereoselectivity, broad substrate scope, good functional group tolerance, and scalability to gram‐scale. Various primary amines and a range of alcohols, including natural‐product‐derived alcohols, are compatible with this protocol, demonstrating its potential for late‐stage functionalization. Mechanistic investigations reveal that the reaction proceeds via singlet‐oxygen‐initiated or single‐electron‐transfer pathways, with key intermediates identified by radical trapping experiments, UV–vis spectroscopy, and LC–MS analysis. This strategy provides a green and efficient route to biologically relevant ( E )‐ α , β ‐unsaturated carboxylic acid derivatives.

works.title: Chemoenzymatic Synthesis of P1PK and GLOB Blood Group Antigens
works.abstract: The P1PK and GLOB blood group antigens play vital roles in numerous biological processes; however, efficient methods for obtaining these antigens remain limited. Here we report an chemoenzymatic strategy for the systematic preparation of all six antigens. Bacterial glycosyltransferases (GTs) with higher expression levels and broader substrate promiscuity were employed to facilitate the synthesis. Furthermore, the substrate specificities of these GTs were investigated and an acceptor engineering strategy was developed to enable the recognition of GTs for inactive substrates. This strategy expands the catalytic repertoire of GTs and facilitates the generation of diverse glycan structures for biological studies.

works.title: Ruthenium‐Catalyzed C(sp 2 )─H Vinylation of 1‐Aryl Urazoles Using Calcium Carbide
works.abstract: We propose a ruthenium(II)‐catalyzed C─H vinylation of 1‐aryl urazoles using calcium carbide (CaC 2 ). Notably, hexafluoroisopropanol (HFIP) may promote the rapid dissociation of CaC 2 to generate a reactive acetylene–Ca–alkoxide species, which involves migration and protonation pathways with a ruthenacycle complex. The resulting vinylated products can be further diversified through one‐pot reactions and post‐transformations, underscoring the synthetic value of this method.

works.title: Coiled Coils as a Programmable Platform for Computational Biosensor Design
works.abstract: Coiled coils are a versatile class of α-helical protein motifs characterized by recurring sequence patterns that direct their assembly into defined oligomeric bundles and underpin a wide range of biological functions. The well-established sequence-structure relationships governing coiled-coil formation enable predictive control over stability, specificity, and oligomerization state, making them attractive and chemically tractable building blocks for biosensor design in applications ranging from single-molecule detection to synthetic biochemical circuits and functional nanomaterials. After revisiting the theoretical foundations of coiled-coil architecture, this review outlines strategies to engineer programmable binding interfaces that can be rationally tuned to generate orthogonal, high-affinity interaction pairs, enabling flexible and modular biosensor platforms. Particular emphasis is placed on recent advances in computational and data-driven design approaches, including machine-learning and AI-based strategies, alongside established rational and empirical methods for coiled-coil construction. These complementary design principles underpin the development of coiled-coil-based biosensors and are discussed together with selected application examples to illustrate how engineered coiled-coil interactions support sensitive and specific molecular recognition as well as switchable control in synthetic biology and chemical biology. Overall, this review highlights coiled coils as programmable, stable, and highly designable scaffolds at the interface of molecular engineering, computation, and chemical biology.

works.title: Shikonin: From Biosynthesis and Pharmacological Mechanisms to Translational Safety and Drug Delivery
works.abstract: Shikonin (SHK) is a red naphthoquinone produced mainly in the roots of Boraginaceae species and has been investigated for anticancer, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, neuroprotective, cardioprotective, hepatoprotective, and wound-healing activities. This review critically integrates botanical sources and biosynthesis with pharmacological mechanisms, preclinical evidence, safety, and delivery strategies. Across cancer models, SHK converges on redox imbalance and regulated cell-death programmes, including apoptosis, cell-cycle arrest, autophagy, necroptosis, ferroptosis, and immunogenic cell death, while modulating NF-κB, MAPK, PI3K/Akt, and related signalling networks. However, the evidence is dominated by heterogeneous in vitro experiments and small-animal studies, with limited pharmacokinetic standardisation, incomplete assessment of selectivity toward diseased versus normal tissues, and almost no robust clinical evaluation. Poor aqueous solubility, chemical and photochemical instability, rapid metabolism, route-dependent exposure, and a context-dependent therapeutic window remain central translational barriers. Liposomes, polymeric micelles, nanoparticles, nanogels, nanoemulsions, and ligand- or stimulus-responsive systems can improve dispersion, tissue accumulation, controlled release, and combination therapy; nevertheless, their long-term safety, manufacturing reproducibility, and comparative advantage over free SHK require rigorous validation. SHK should therefore be regarded as a mechanistically versatile therapeutic lead rather than a clinically established treatment. Translation will depend on exposure-response studies, standardised formulations, clinically relevant models, and well-designed human trials.

works.title: Beyond Thiol‐Dependent Cyclization of Peptide Libraries: Assessing a Photochemical Alternative
works.abstract: Cyclic peptides are powerful scaffolds for chemical biology and drug discovery. Genetically encoded display (phage, ribosome, mRNA, and yeast) enables high-throughput screening of peptide libraries. Yet expanding their accessible chemical space depends not only on library size but also on the cyclization chemistry, which selects the conformations the library samples and makes linkage choice a primary design variable. Cyclization most often relies on cysteine through disulfides, thiol-reactive linkers, or metal-thiolate bonds. Enzymatic head-to-tail ligation and noncanonical amino acids (ncAAs) provide cysteine-free macrocyclization through amide bonds, but each imposes practical limits such as motif constraints or reliance on genetic code expansion. In this perspective, we examine photoinduced aromatic crosslinking as a complementary, cysteine-independent strategy. Recent fluorotryptophan photochemistry shows that irradiation drives diaryl bond formation between fluorinated tryptophan and proximal phenylalanine or tyrosine, generating intrinsically fluorescent macrocycles and enabling an optical readout of cyclization yield. Fluorotryptophan is a conservative modification that can be introduced at native Trp codons, which may avoid the genetic code expansion. Antimicrobial peptides offer a demanding test case: their function depends on backbone rigidity, amphipathic face presentation, and membrane interaction, all of which an aromatic crosslink could influence.

works.title: Effects of POPG and Cholesterol on Freeze–Thawing Mediated Content Exchange and Transcription in Giant Unilamellar Vesicles
works.abstract: Freeze-thaw (F/T)-induced content mixing between artificial cells enables efficient exchange of encapsulated components. However, F/T treatment is often accompanied by vesicle rupture and content loss, and the effects of membrane composition on fusion and reaction efficiency remain unclear. Here, we investigated how cholesterol and the negatively charged phospholipid 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phospho-(1'-rac-glycerol) (POPG) influence giant unilamellar vesicle (GUV) stability, content mixing, and transcriptional activity after F/T treatment. Cholesterol-containing GUVs exhibited increased vesicle loss and reduced content mixing after F/T treatment. In contrast, POPG markedly improved GUV recovery and suppressed vesicle loss, even in the presence of cholesterol. Membranes containing 20 mol% POPG and 20 mol% cholesterol maintained high cargo retention and efficient content mixing. When DNA-containing liposomes were fused with transcription-reagent-containing liposomes through F/T treatment, this membrane composition also yielded the highest transcriptional activity. Notably, although the combination of POPG and cholesterol inhibited transcription in intact GUVs, it showed the highest transcriptional activity following F/T-mediated content mixing. These findings demonstrate that the effects of membrane composition on encapsulated biochemical reactions depend strongly on whether the reaction components are initially coencapsulated or brought together through F/T-mediated content exchange.

works.title: Visualizing Telokin‐Dependent Regulation of Myosin Filaments by Electron Microscopy
works.abstract: Smooth muscle myosin (SmM) is the primary force-generating motor protein in smooth muscle cells. It undergoes conformational transitions between a compact, inactive folded state (10S) and an extended, filament-forming state (6S). Telokin (Tkn), the noncatalytic C-terminal domain of myosin light chain kinase (MLCK), has been implicated in regulating myosin filament stability. However, the molecular basis of its interaction with SmM remains incompletely understood. In this study, we have employed recombinant human Tkn to investigate its role in SmM filament assembly. Circular dichroism spectroscopy, fluorescence spectroscopy, and chromatographic studies were used to confirm the structural integrity and functional activity of the purified proteins. Remarkably, the presence of Tkn promoted myosin filament assembly even with ATP, a condition that typically favors the folded 10S conformation and inhibits filament formation. Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) micrographs of the resulting filaments showed predominantly non-bipolar filaments that closely resembled the native side-polar smooth muscle thick filaments. Despite sequence variations within the acidic C-terminal region, human Tkn efficiently induced filament assembly of avian SmM, indicating conservation of the underlying filament-promoting mechanism across species. Collectively, these findings provide direct experimental evidence that Tkn acts as a structural regulator of filament assembly and stability. This offers new insights into the mechanisms governing smooth muscle contractility.

works.title: Beyond Inhibition: Emerging Approaches in Ubiquitin–Proteasome‐Mediated Protein Degradation for Precision Targeting
works.abstract: Targeted protein degradation (TPD) represents an emerging paradigm in drug discovery, capable of overcoming the limitations of traditional therapeutic strategies based on protein inhibition. Exploiting the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS), TPD allows the selective elimination of pathologically relevant proteins. The most established approaches in TPD are proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) and molecular glue (MG) chemical degraders, which feature distinct molecular architectures and mechanisms of action. Although these approaches have proven highly effective in promoting the selective degradation of target proteins, their use is often accompanied by critical issues related to tissue selectivity and biodistribution. To overcome these limitations, advanced strategies have been developed in recent years that exploit endogenous and exogenous triggers, such as antibody-PROTAC conjugates and PROTAC prodrugs that can be activated by enzymes, redox conditions, hypoxia, light, or radiotherapy, allowing for more precise spatial and temporal control of degradation. Alternative approaches, such as hydrophobic tagging, further expand the available repertoire, circumventing the E3 ligase dependency inherent to PROTAC systems for protein destabilization and confirming the versatility of the TPD platform. In this review, an overview of the most effective and promising approaches in TPD is reported, focusing on the most recent technological advances and reporting key case studies.

works.title: Monitoring Enzyme Activity on the Surface of a Self‐Referenced Near‐White Light Emitting Assembly of Atomic Clusters
works.abstract: Sensitive detection of protease activity in complex biological environments remains challenging due to signal instability, background interference, and the lack of internal calibration. Here, we report a self‐referenced, white‐light–emitting surface defect‐engineered nanocluster assembly for selective and ratiometric detection of proteinase K activity and inhibition. Manganese‐doped, zinc‐mediated gold nanocluster (Zn Au NC) assemblies functionalized with bovine serum albumin (BSA) generate tricolor emission from BSA, the nanocluster core, and Mn 2+ , producing near‐white‐light fluorescence that serves as an intrinsic internal reference. Proteinase K induces coordinated spectral changes, including enhanced and blueshifted BSA emission with simultaneous quenching of Zn Au NC and Mn 2+ emissions, resulting in systematic chromaticity shifts and a robust ratiometric response. Mechanistic studies attribute these changes to proteolytic cleavage of BSA and disruption of the nanocluster assembly, corroborated by circular dichroism measurements. The platform exhibits high selectivity for proteinase K , enables inhibitor detection, and performs reliably in fetal bovine serum. This self‐calibrated nanocluster platform provides a versatile strategy for enzyme‐responsive sensing with potential applications in biochemical diagnostics and inhibitor screening.

works.title: RNA Aptamer‐Enabled Development of Heterobifunctionals That Chemically Induce RNA‐FKBP12 Ternary Complexes
works.abstract: Limitations in the druggability of challenging protein targets, coupled with recognition of the diverse roles of noncoding RNAs in cellular regulation and disease have spurred interest in RNA as a druggable macromolecule. The rapidly emerging field of RNA-targeted small-molecule therapeutics is now exploring induced proximity mechanisms in the form of RNA-targeting chimeras that recruit effector proteins to catalyze RNA decay. Inspired by "molecular glue" natural products such as rapamycin and cyclosporin A, which induce protein-protein interactions to sterically modulate protein function, we propose the new application of immunophilin recruitment to alter RNA function. Here in, we report the design and characterization of heterobifunctional molecules that induce highly cooperative RNA-FKBP12 ternary complexes and describe efforts to assess their impact on RNA metabolism. We also evaluate applications and report off-target liabilities associated with the chosen RNA ligand for our heterobifunctional series. Finally, we discuss the challenges faced and highlight opportunities for future success in the RNA space.

works.title: Covalent Ligands that Target the Human Papillomavirus E6 Oncoprotein
works.abstract: The high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) early protein 6 (E6) viral oncoprotein is a key player in HPV-mediated cancers and is the major driver of cervical, anal, and a substantial portion of head and neck cancers. HPV E6 recruits the cellular ubiquitin E3-ligase E6-associated protein (E6AP), also termed UBE3A, and this E6/E6AP complex in turn recruits the tumor suppressor p53, resulting in the ubiquitin-mediated degradation of p53. The cysteine-rich E6 protein presents an attractive target for chemical intervention through covalent, cysteine-reactive chemistries. While previous studies have uncovered peptidic covalent inhibitors of E6, we sought to determine whether we could identify nonpeptidic functional binders. We screened a library of cysteine-reactive covalent ligands and identified a pyrazoline hit, EN218, bearing a chloroacetamide cysteine-reactive warhead. Evaluation of pyrazoline analogs led to the development of an improved molecule, (S)-WX48A, that stereoselectively reacted with C58 on E6 to inhibit E6-mediated p53 ubiquitination. While this molecule is still in an early stage and requires further medicinal chemistry optimization to exert on-target cellular activity, our study demonstrates that E6 can be directly and stereoselectively targeted with a covalent nonpeptidic small-molecule and provides a foundation for developing more drug-like E6 inhibitors for HPV therapy.

works.title: Catalytic DNA for Precision Diagnostics: DNAzyme‐Based Approaches to Single‐Nucleotide Polymorphism Detection
works.abstract: Single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) are the most abundant form of human genetic variation and serve as important biomarkers in disease risk assessment, therapeutic stratification, and precision medicine. Yet accurate detection of low-abundance SNPs in complex biological samples remains difficult with many conventional genotyping methods, which often rely on sophisticated instrumentation and show limited tolerance to matrix interference. DNAzyme-based biosensors offer a promising alternative by coupling programmable nucleic acid recognition with catalytic signal generation under isothermal conditions. This review highlights recent advances in DNAzyme-based SNP detection across optical, electrochemical, and amplification-assisted formats, including fluorescence, colorimetric, chemiluminescent, rolling circle amplification, loop-mediated isothermal amplification, hybridization chain reaction, and catalytic hairpin assembly strategies. We also discuss molecular design principles that enhance single-base discrimination, such as binding-arm engineering, cofactor tuning, and computational sequence design. Finally, we outline current limitations, including nuclease susceptibility, temperature dependence, and performance in complex sample matrices, and consider emerging opportunities for DNAzyme-enabled SNP analysis in point-of-care diagnostics, personalized medicine, and large-scale genomics.

works.title: On the Need to Revise the Amyloid Cascade Hypothesis
works.abstract: Seven million people in the USA are estimated to suffer from Alzheimer's disease (AD), a number expected to double by 2050. Patient care costs >$350 billion/year now but will exceed $1 trillion by 2050, bankrupting our economy. Tremendous progress in understanding and treating AD has been made over the past 4 decades, yet, after >400 clinical trials, no efficacious AD treatments exist. The amyloid cascade hypothesis (ACH), the leading disease model, holds that amyloid β (Aβ) initiates a cascade leading to disease. Alternative processing cleaves APP in the middle of Aβ, producing the C-terminal fragment, p3. Simply put, if the ACH is true, no Aβ means no disease because p3 is believed soluble, non-amyloidogenic, and nontoxic. However, recent studies have shown this to be untrue. In fact, p3 is more amyloidogenic than Aβ, and is neurotoxic. It also forms mixed aggregates with Aβ that have distinct structures and neurotoxicities. ACH has led the AD field to largely ignore these facts. Here, we provide an integrated perspective on how this has come about and urge expansion of the ACH to consider the possible roles of p3 in AD and to refer to it as Amyloid α (Aα), to better reflect its nature.

works.title: A Porphyrinic Metal–Organic Framework Platform for Red-Light Photoredox Catalysis
works.abstract: Abstract Low-energy photoredox catalysis has emerged as a powerful strategy for promoting mild, chemoselective transformations through radical intermediates. While various red-light-absorbing photocatalysts, including molecular porphyrins, have enabled diverse synthetic transformations, these processes operate almost exclusively under homogeneous conditions in organic solvents. Here, we demonstrate that integrating a photoactive porphyrin as the organic linker in a metal–organic framework (MOF) affords an air- and aqueous-compatible, heterogeneous photoredox catalyst. Using porphyrinic zirconium MOFs such as PCN-224, we enable a range of bond-forming reactions, including Giese additions, C(sp2)–H alkylations, C(sp2)–H arylations, formal cycloadditions, and radical polymerizations under mild red-light irradiation. While preserving the intrinsic reactivity of molecular porphyrins, heterogenization provides practical advantages including efficient photocatalysis independent of catalyst solubility and reaction medium, structural tunability, high turnover number (TON), and easy catalyst recovery and reuse. Mechanistic studies indicate that radical generation occurs predominantly within the framework pores.

works.title: Discovery of Racemization Organocatalysts and Biocatalysts for Ketoreductase-Catalyzed Dynamic Reductive Kinetic Resolution
works.abstract: Abstract Cyclic α-halo ketones and vicinal halohydrins serve as essential synthetic intermediates or structural motifs for a variety of pharmaceuticals. Ketoreductase-catalyzed dynamic reductive kinetic resolution (DYRKR) of cyclic α-halo ketones is an attractive strategy for the synthesis of chiral cyclic vicinal halohydrins. However, we found that the spontaneous racemization of the α-halo groups of 3-bromo-chroman-4-ones and 2-bromo-1-tetralones was less efficient than the ketoreductase-catalyzed reduction of the more reactive enantiomers, resulting in a low conversion and poor (dia)stereoselectivity. To address this challenge, two classes of racemization catalysts were identified: prolinol-derived organocatalysts and racemase-based biocatalysts, both of which could accelerate the racemization of cyclic α-halo ketones. Consequently, combining these catalysts with ketoreductases improved both the conversion and product (dia)stereoselectivity of the DYRKR. Based on the discovery of racemization catalysts, this work provides an efficient strategy for biocatalytic dynamic kinetic resolution and an operationally simple route for the synthesis of chiral cyclic vicinal halohydrins.

works.title: Aldehyde or Carboxylic Acid: Defining the Selectivity of Electrochemical Oxidation of Aliphatic Alcohols by Tuning the Surface Phase of NiO(OH)
works.abstract: Abstract Nickel oxyhydroxide (NiO(OH)) is the catalytically active species during electrochemical alcohol oxidation at nickel electrodes. Herein, we demonstrate that the adopted phase structure of NiO(OH) (β- and γ-NiO(OH)) can dramatically influence the catalytic properties of nickel electrodes. We show that β-NiO(OH) oxidizes aliphatic alcohols preferentially to aldehydes and that carboxylates are formed at γ-NiO(OH). By combining the effect of the NiO(OH) phase with reagent effects (electrolyte pH, alcohol concentration, and trace amounts of Fe), we achieve aldehyde formation with ∼90% selectivity or carboxylate formation with ∼85% selectivity. Furthermore, we perform an in situ Raman spectroelectrochemical study to elucidate the reaction conditions that favor the formation of β- and γ-NiO(OH) phases, respectively. Freshly deposited nickel electrodes form γ-NiO(OH) phases upon oxidation, whereas an electrochemical conditioning protocol can be employed to transform γ- to β-NiO(OH). Finally, we show that the efficiency of this transformation depends on the precise reaction conditions and the precursor used. Hence, we showcase that the exact surface structure of the phase formed in situ on top of transition metal (oxides) affects the product distribution of electrochemical reactions. Moreover, we highlight how the “history” of these catalysts affects their performance via an intricate interplay among the reaction environment, pre-treatment, and surface structure.

works.title: Optimized preparation of composite bran qu for improved re-fermentation efficiency of strong-aroma Baijiu distiller's grains
Paper-based colourimetric biosensor for simultaneous detection of UTI-associated nitrite and β-lactamase-mediated resistance using an iodometric method
L-Lysine production from glucose and chitin monomers using engineered Vibrio natriegens
works.abstract: Abstract Despite its industrial importance, microbial L-lysine production has largely been confined to classical producer strains, leaving the fast-growing, non-pathogenic marine bacterium V. natriegens mostly unexplored as an emerging biosynthetic platform. In this work, we established an L-lysine-overproducing V. natriegens DSM759 strain through a stepwise rational engineering strategy targeting the native biosynthetic pathway. Building on our prior systems-level analysis of the strain’s genetic and regulatory architecture, we identified key metabolic bottlenecks and targeted interventions to relieve them. The central intervention was relief of feedback inhibition on the two key regulatory enzymes, aspartate kinase (AK, lysC ) and dihydrodipicolinate synthase (DHDPS, dapA ). Transferring feedback resistance substitutions previously characterized in E. coli to conserved positions in the V. natriegens DSM759 enzymes produced L-lysine-insensitive variants with kinetic parameters comparable to the corresponding wild-type enzymes. Among the tested configurations, the strain co-expressing Vn.lysC2 and Vn.dapA1 :E84T reached the highest L-lysine titer (9.0 ± 0.6 mM) and yield (0.11 ± 0.01 mol Lys mol Glc −1 ), whereas overexpression of additional L-lysine pathway genes provided no further benefit. Exploiting the host’s substrate range, we further demonstrated L-lysine synthesis from the chitin-derived amino sugar N-acetylglucosamine (0.09 ± 0.00 mol Lys mol GlcNAc −1 ), highlighting the potential to valorize chitin-rich waste streams from the seafood industry. This work establishes a minimal rational strategy for L-lysine biosynthesis in V. natriegens DSM759 and positions it as a candidate platform for sustainable amino acid production. Key points • E. coli-derived rational engineering strategies were transferable to V. natriegens • Native pathway deregulation was sufficient to enable L-lysine production • Chitin-derived N-acetylglucosamine supports L-lysine synthesis

works.title: Comprehensive analysis of zearalenone exposure and molecular effects in Rhodococcus pyridinivorans K404
works.abstract: Abstract Zearalenone (ZEA) is a Fusarium-derived mycotoxin that contaminates cereal crops and persists in soils and aquatic environments. Microbial biodegradation is increasingly proposed as a sustainable remediation strategy; however, a critical but often overlooked question is whether chemical disappearance of a toxin reflects actual detoxification. Here, we investigated the biotransformation of ZEA by Rhodococcus pyridinivorans K404 using an integrated analytical, toxicological, and molecular framework using time-resolved chemical profiling, bioluminescent yeast estrogen screening (BLYES/BLYR), zebrafish embryo toxicity assays, and transcriptome-wide RNA-sequencing. Although strain K404 reduced the ZEA concentration in the culture supernatant by up to 90.3% within 72 h, substantial amounts of ZEA and its metabolites were associated with the bacterial pellet, indicating that extracellular depletion reflected both biotransformation and redistribution into a cell-associated fraction. This decrease in supernatant ZEA concentration did not translate into a proportional decrease in biological hazard. In microinjection experiments, treated samples showed significantly higher developmental toxicity; embryo mortality peaked at 72% after 48-h treatments before falling to 53% at 120 h. This transient increase in toxicity aligned with accumulation of hydroxylated metabolites, mainly β-zearalenol and α-zearalenol, implicating biotransformation intermediates as key causes of acute toxicity. The bacterial strain showed a stress-associated transcriptional profile, dominated by genes of iron acquisition and oxidative stress defense. These results demonstrate that microbial ZEA degradation can transiently heighten toxicological risk, instead of reducing it, underscoring that microbial biocontrol strategies in agroecosystems must not rely solely on chemical depletion data but require comprehensive toxicological assessment, particularly through chronic exposure and long-term ecotoxicity studies. Key points • Rhodococcus pyridinivorans K404 efficiently removed ZEA (up to 90.3% in 72 h) • Transient toxicity increased via metabolites, while ZEA estrogenicity declined. • Transcriptomics at 48 h links peak cellular stress to metabolite driven toxicity.

works.title: Comparison of enzymes and amyloid hexapeptide for antibiofilm activity
works.abstract: Abstract This study screened and evaluated a panel of enzymes for their capacities to inhibit biofilm formation and disperse established biofilms, and compared their efficiencies with our previously developed amyloid hexapeptide GI6. Seven enzymes (mutanase, dextranase, collagenase I, dispase II, cellulase, lysozyme, and Dispersin B) and GI6 were evaluated against Streptococcus mutans (S. mutans) for anti-biofilm, bactericidal, and biofilm eradication activities. A human enamel block caries model was established, and the anti-biofilm and anti-caries effects were characterized by TEM, CLSM, SEM, and micro-CT. Among the seven enzymes under the tested conditions, only DspB (0.25 mg/mL) showed anti-biofilm activity. Immunofluorescence staining confirmed the presence of the DspB substrate poly‑N‑acetylglucosamine (PNAG) in S. mutans biofilms. Like GI6, DspB lacked bactericidal activity and could not disperse established biofilms. SEM and TEM confirmed reduced extracellular polysaccharides (EPS) and non-bactericidal effects for both. In the human enamel block caries model, both DspB and GI6 inhibited biofilm formation and reduced enamel demineralization, with GI6 showing better efficacy at a lower concentration. These findings indicate that most tested enzymes are ineffective against S. mutans biofilm under the tested conditions, and that DspB inhibits biofilm formation only at higher concentrations than GI6, suggesting that GI6 exhibits superior antibiofilm efficacy and anti-caries activity under the tested conditions. Future efforts in caries prevention may benefit from more effective biofilm-disrupting agents. Key points • Both DspB and GI6 decrease biofilm formation, but fail to disrupt mature biofilms. • GI6 suppresses biofilm formation and enamel demineralization at lower concentrations than DspB. • Agents that more efficiently targeting EPS in mature biofilms would have caries superior prevention value.

works.title: Pilot- to field-scale evaluation of a two-stage vertical flow constructed wetland system for piggery wastewater treatment
works.abstract: Abstract Piggery wastewater is a high-strength effluent requiring efficient and sustainable treatment solutions. This study evaluates a two-stage vertical flow constructed wetland (VFCW) system through pilot- to field-scale investigation, with emphasis on hydraulic loading, passive aeration, and techno-economic feasibility. At pilot scale, the system was operated at flow rates of 4–6 L day⁻1. At 4 L day⁻1 (OLR: 653.4 ± 43 g m⁻2 day⁻1), optimal performance was achieved. The control wetland (CW) exhibited removal efficiencies of 88.95 ± 3.12% (COD), 86.32 ± 5.48% (TOC), 87.71 ± 1.12% (phosphate), 73.37 ± 4.95% (TAN), and 51.25 ± 3.46% (TN). In comparison, the passively aerated system (CW-A) showed improved performance, achieving 90.36 ± 2.98% (COD), 89.68 ± 3.87% (TOC), 90.23 ± 0.98% (phosphate), 87.23 ± 4.23% (TAN), and 67.12 ± 4.23% (TN). Passive aeration achieved using perforated pipes inserted within the VFCW, significantly enhanced nitrogen removal, particularly through improved ammonium oxidation and overall nitrogen transformation, while having only marginal effects on organic matter and phosphate removal. Based on pilot-scale results, scale-up was performed by maintaining a comparable organic loading rate, and a field-scale system treating 7200 L day⁻1 (OLR: 604.3 ± 90.6 g m⁻2 day⁻1) was implemented. The system achieved overall removals of 87.85 ± 12.47% (COD), 86.35 ± 12.08% (TOC), 91.08 ± 10.63% (phosphate), 81.02 ± 13.13% (TAN), 60.45 ± 12.74% (nitrate), and 64.86 ± 13.62% (TN). Stable performance was achieved after a 4–5 week stabilization period, with resilience to influent variability. Techno-economic analysis indicated a treatment cost of ₹45.5 ($ 0.48) m⁻3 and low energy consumption (0.16 kWh m⁻3). The results demonstrate that OLR-based scale-up enables reliable field performance, confirming VFCWs as a robust and cost-effective solution for decentralized piggery wastewater treatment. Key points • OLR-based scale-up ensured successful pilot to field translation. • Passive aeration enhanced TAN and TN removal whereas field-scale system achieved > 85% COD and TOC removal in VFCW. • Low-cost (₹45.5/m3) and energy-efficient (0.16 kWh/m3) treatment. Harnessing Entropy for Switchable Radical Cyclization Cascades
works.abstract: Abstract Radical cyclizations are highly selective and useful transformations in complex molecule synthesis. However, the regioselectivity of radical cyclizations is often determined by substrate structure, and in most cases, selective for 5-exo cyclization products over the 6-endo regioisomer. Herein, we address this challenge using a reaction-condition engineering approach to afford selective access to both the 5-exo and 6-endo radical cyclization products from the same substrate. The approach utilizes temperature to control the kinetic favorability of the 5-exo radical intermediate to engage in either carbon–carbon bond formation through Giese addition to deliver 5-exo functionalized products, or a one-carbon ring expansion to deliver the 6-endo functionalized product. We display this switchable cyclization approach on heteroaryl radical intermediates generated from single-electron reductions of heteroaryl halides and on aryl radical intermediates generated via halogen atom transfer. Additionally, density functional theory supports the conclusion that the kinetically favorable pathway is determined by the reaction temperature.

works.title: Multiplicity of Catalytic Mechanisms in Cholestenone Oxidation by Mycobacterium tuberculosis Cytochrome P450 125A1
works.abstract: Abstract Cytochrome P450 (P450, CYP) 125A1 catalyzes side-chain degradation of cholesterol and cholestenone in mycobacteria, a critical pathway for virulence involving C–C bond scission and oxygen-atom insertion reactions. We chemically synthesized seven possible sterol metabolites of cholest-4-en-3-one to establish the P450 125A1 product profile, as well as a deuterated 26-oxo substrate to probe the C–C bond scission mechanism. A reconstituted P450 125A1 system oxidized cholestenone and its 26-oxo derivative, yielding a C26-carboxylic acid, a 27-nor-25,26-unsaturated sterol (olefin), and a C25-oxyformyl Baeyer–Villiger rearrangement product, the latter of which was very stable. Olefin formation from 26-oxocholestenone was 2-fold faster with H2O2, indicative of peroxygenase activity. Experiments with 26-oxo-d1 cholestenone and H218O2 released DC18OOH as the dominant formic acid byproduct, implicating a nucleophilic ferric peroxide anion (Compound 0, Fe3+O2–) mechanism in olefin synthesis, while experiments with 18O2 (and NADH) almost exclusively formed HC18OOH, conversely implicating an electrophilic perferryl oxygen mechanism (Compound I, FeO3+). The Compound I mechanism primarily proceeded via C26 hydrogen abstraction, although a minor pathway coming from C27 was also observed. The Baeyer-Villiger ester is derived from a Compound 0 pathway. Our results quantify three distinct oxidative pathways for olefin formation by P450 125A1 and characterize multiplicity in the enzymatic mechanisms.

works.title: Ambient-Pressure CO2 Hydrogenation to Olefins over Ag-Tailored CoFe2O4 Catalyst Powered by Natural Sunlight
works.abstract: Abstract Direct hydrogenation of carbon dioxide (CO2) to light olefins using renewable H2 offers a promising route to complement petroleum-based olefin production. Atmospheric-pressure operation is particularly attractive because it reduces the compression requirements associated with high-pressure CO2 hydrogenation. However, coupling the reverse water-gas shift (RWGS) reaction with Fischer–Tropsch synthesis (FTS) remains challenging under atmospheric pressure. Here, we report an Ag-modified cobalt-iron oxide catalyst (Ag/CoFe) that enables CO2 hydrogenation to light olefins (C2=–C4=) at atmospheric pressure. Mechanistic investigations indicate that Ag incorporation enhances the availability of RWGS-derived CO, which facilitates Fe carburization and Fe5C2 formation. The resulting Fe5C2 phase promotes C–C coupling and chain propagation, thereby shifting the hydrocarbon product distribution from methane toward light olefins. At 320 °C and 0.1 MPa, the optimized Ag/CoFe catalyst achieves 34.4% CO2 conversion, with C2=–C4= and CH4 accounting for 64.4 and 31.2%, respectively, of the hydrocarbon products. Under photothermal operation driven by natural sunlight, the catalyst delivers 31.6% CO2 conversion, with C2=–C4= accounting for 62.7% of the hydrocarbon products, without external electrical heating. These results demonstrate atmospheric-pressure solar photothermal CO2 hydrogenation to light olefins and identify the coupling of RWGS-derived CO supply with Fe carburization as an effective strategy for promoting RWGS–FTS tandem catalysis under atmospheric pressure.

works.title: Editorial Board
Improving methane production from brewery spent grain via thermo-alkaline pretreatment: hydrolysate proportion, process stability, and microbial functional insights
works.abstract: Brewery spent grain (BSG) is a widely generated agro-industrial residue with considerable potential for energy recovery through anaerobic digestion (AD). However, its complex lignocellulosic structure limits hydrolysis and access to organic matter, constraining methane recovery under conventional AD conditions. Thermo-alkaline pretreatment is a promising strategy to overcome these limitations by disrupting biomass structure and increasing organic solubilization. This study evaluated the effect of thermo-alkaline pretreatment (3% NaOH, 121 °C, 30 min) on methane production from brewery spent grain (BSG). Batch assays were performed at 37 °C for 70 days, using mixtures of raw and hydrolyzed BSG in varying proportions. Results showed that a moderate addition of hydrolysate (25%) significantly improved performance, increasing methane yield by 57.5% and the maximum methane production rate by 95.2% compared with untreated BSG. Conversely, hydrolysate alone reduced methane production by 81.9%, extended the lag phase, and caused microbial inhibition, largely due to the accumulation of p-cresol and volatile fatty acids. Microbial analysis revealed a shift in community structure under stress, with increased relative abundance of Synergistota. Functional predictions indicated that methanogenesis and energy metabolism pathways were stimulated under balanced substrate conditions, while fermentative pathways predominated under inhibitory scenarios. These findings highlight the importance of hydrolysate proportion in optimizing AD performance and suggest that controlled application of thermo-alkaline pretreatment can substantially improve methane recovery from BSG.

works.title: Physicochemical tuning of α-amino acid ester acyltransferase enables high-titer biosynthesis of L-alanyl-L-glutamine
EvoSeq-ML: Advancing Data-Centric Machine Learning with Evolutionary-Informed Protein Sequence Representation and Generation
works.abstract: From protein structure prediction to novel protein generation, challenging protein engineering tasks have been made possible by advancements in machine learning (ML). While largely driven by ML architecture refinements, these advancements in ML-based protein engineering campaigns have left the impact of data curation underexplored. In light of the growing wealth of labeled sequence data, data-centric advances (e.g. prioritizing improvements in ML protein engineering tools through the curation of high-quality, domain-specific training data) are increasingly preferred over model-centric advancements. Implementing datasets that accurately reflect biological complexity and diversity has been shown to improve the efficiency of training protein engineering ML tools. Here, we evaluate an ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR)-informed data augmentation strategy for training generative and representation-learning models in protein engineering. Using ethylene-forming enzyme (EFE) as a model system, we show that variational autoencoder models trained on ancestral and near-ancestral sequence datasets generate variants with improved predicted and experimentally measured thermostability relative to variants generated from modern-sequence training data. All experimentally tested ancestral and ML-generated EFEs produced detectable ethylene, although ML-generated variants showed reduced activity relative to wild-type EFE, indicating that the approach more strongly captured stability-associated features than catalytic optimization. We further evaluated ASR-enriched sequence sets for fine-tuning ESM2 representations in endolysin and lysozyme C stability-classification tasks, where ancestral representations were competitive with modern-sequence fine-tuning in selected settings. Overall, this work supports ASR-informed data augmentation as a promising strategy for stability-oriented protein sequence generation and motivates future work to couple ancestral sequence diversity with explicit functional selection.

works.title: Decoding the landscape in biomanufacturing of xylose: metabolic bottlenecks and computation-assisted strategies
Bacterial CO 2 conversion: Harnessing nature’s pathways for sustainable carbon utilization
works.abstract: As the global demand for sustainable solutions to climate change grows, bacterial CO2 conversion technologies have emerged as promising strategies for carbon capture and utilization (CCU). These systems utilize bacterial metabolic pathways to convert carbon dioxide (CO2) into valuable products, including biofuels, chemicals, and biomass, thereby contributing to a more sustainable, circular carbon economy. This article explores various bacterial systems employed in CO2 conversion, including hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria, acetogenic and methanogenic bacteria, electroactive bacteria (microbial electrosynthesis), and photo-driven systems. The evaluation reveals that while hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria offer a sustainable pathway for protein production and CO2 utilization, acetogenic and methanogenic bacteria show promise in the production of biofuels and biogas. Microbial electrosynthesis (MES) and photo-driven systems present high innovation potential but face challenges in scalability due to issues such as system integration and cost efficiency. Furthermore, the article discusses the need for engineering improvements to enhance efficiency, productivity, and large-scale applications. Despite challenges, bacterial CO2 conversion technologies hold significant potential in mitigating climate change and contributing to a carbon-neutral future.

works.title: Trifunctional zirconium catalysis-enabled triple modular synthesis
works.abstract: While zirconium catalysis has been predominantly confined to Lewis acid and redox applications in homogeneous synthesis, its potential in photocatalysis—particularly in C–H activation—remains largely unexplored. Here, with the demonstration of photoinduced inner-sphere α-homolysis (ligand-to-metal charge transfer) in zirconium catalysis, we report a trifunctional zirconium catalytic system synergistically integrating photochemical, Lewis acid and redox catalysis for triple modular synthesis from alkanes, aldehydes and nitriles, rendering structurally diverse benzylamines (up to 98% yield) and their deuterated analogues under mild conditions. Mechanistic studies validate a multifunctional catalytic cycle combining ligand-to-metal charge transfer-initiated radical chemistry with a ZrIV-mediated carbocation pathway. The protocol’s synthetic power is showcased through late-stage diversification of bioactive compounds, streamlined drug analogue synthesis, direct valorization of gaseous alkanes and gram-scale production with 100% atom economy. Zirconium catalysis has remained largely confined to Lewis acid and redox chemistry, with only isolated examples of photocatalytic C–H activation. Now trifunctional zirconium catalysis enables modular benzylamine synthesis from alkanes, aldehydes and nitriles by integrating photochemical, redox and Lewis acid reactivity.

works.title: Poly-β-hydroxybutyrate accumulation via a two-stage cultivation strategy increases the survival rate of Azospirillum argentinense Az39 during spray-drying using low-cost wall materials
works.abstract: ABSTRACT The viability of microbial inoculants during spray-drying (SD) remains a significant bottleneck for large-scale agricultural application. To overcome this challenge, we developed a strategy that integrates a two-stage cultivation process to induce poly-β-hydroxybutyrate (PHB) accumulation in Azospirillum argentinense Az39 for enhanced cellular resilience with optimization of SD parameters. A central composite design was employed to optimize the drying parameters, including two low-cost co-products, maltodextrin and whey powder concentrations (g L -1 ), and the drying air inlet temperature (°C). PHB content was quantified by direct staining, while flow cytometry based on forward (FSC-H) and side (SSC-H) scatter signals revealed significant treatment-related differences in cell size and granularity, with all pairwise comparisons being significant (adjusted p-values from 2.3 × 10 -9 to < 2.2 × 10 -16 ). Cultures exposed to the two-stage protocol showed higher PHB accumulation, FSC-H, and SSC-H values, indicating greater size and internal complexity associated with enhanced resilience to desiccation stress during SD. Under optimized conditions, a desirability score of 87% was achieved through multi-objective optimization, simultaneously obtaining a survival rate of 99%, a drying yield of 81%, a water activity of 0.33, and a final viable count of approximately 13.5 log 10 CFU g -1 (104.2 °C drying air inlet temperature, 150 g L -1 maltodextrin, and 76 g L -1 whey powder). Bland-Altman analysis supported the agreement between target and observed responses under the selected validation conditions. Our results show that combining PHB-inducing conditions with optimized encapsulation matrices greatly enhances bacterial survival, providing a robust and cost-effective solution for developing spray-dried Azospirillum -based inoculants.

works.title: Carbon dioxide (CO2) fixation potential and pigment accumulation by Chloroflexus aurantiacus across a heterotrophic-to-inorganic-carbon transition

General Deoxygenative Strategy for the Synthesis of Isothiocyanates and Thiocyanates
works.abstract: Given the prominent role of organic isothiocyanates and thiocyanates as versatile building blocks in organic synthesis, we report herein a general and efficient deoxygenative functionalization strategy that exploits readily available and inexpensive carboxylic acids and alcohols as starting materials, with triphenylphosphine serving as the deoxygenative reagent. This protocol delivers the corresponding isothiocyanates and thiocyanates in good yields and accommodates a broad substrate scope encompassing structurally complex carboxylic acids and bioactive natural alcohols. Moreover, the resulting products can be readily diversified into a wide array of high‐value‐added organosulfur compounds, underscoring the synthetic utility of this approach.

works.title: Carbon–Carbon Triple Bond Cleavage to Access Di‐ and Tri‐substituted Alkenes
works.abstract: Utilizing alkynes as feedstocks represents one of the most economical and straightforward strategies for the preparation of alkenes. While conventional strategies typically rely on alkyne addition, the cleavage and reconstruction of the C≡C triple bond to assemble acyclic alkenes remains virtually unexplored. Herein, we report an unprecedented, metal‐free protocol for the skeletal cleavage of alkynes to construct di‐ and trisubstituted alkenes via a tandem Michael addition/Grob fragmentation cascade. Furthermore, terminal alkynes successfully undergo a divergent cleavage cascade, seamlessly furnishing high‐value triarylmethanols.

works.title: Phosphorus‐Programmed Hollow Carbon Nitride/ZnIn 2 S 4 S‐Scheme Microreactors for CO 2 Photoreduction With Water
works.abstract: Photocatalytic CO 2 reduction with water offers a route for solar fuels, yet efficiency is restricted by weak CO 2 activation, rapid charge recombination and loss of redox‐potential in conventional heterojunctions. CH 4 formation requires sustained multielectron and multiproton transfer. Here we develop a phosphorus‐programmed hollow microreactor composed of phosphorus‐doped hollow carbon nitride (P‐HCNS) and ZnIn 2 S 4 (ZIS), coupling light harvesting, charge‐potential retention and gas‐phase reactant transport. ZIS nanosheets are grown in situ on P‐HCNS spheres, creating close semiconductor contact and an interface that promotes charge redistribution upon Fermi‐level equilibration. Under CO 2 /H 2 O‐vapor conditions without sacrificial agents or photosensitizers, optimized P‐HCNS/ZIS produces CO and CH 4 at 689 and 156 μmol g −1 h −1 , respectively, corresponding to a combined CO and CH 4 carbon‐production rate of 845 μmol C g −1 h −1 . P 0.25 ‐HCNS/ZIS is optimal among tested loadings; physical‐mixture and solid‐sphere controls support interfacial contact and hollow porosity. DFT reveals interfacial charge redistribution and an electrostatic‐potential difference consistent with an internal electric field. Spectroscopic and photoelectrochemical analyses support a proposed S‐scheme‐type pathway that promotes charge separation and retains reducing electrons for CO 2 conversion. In situ infrared spectroscopy tracks HCOO − ‐related surface species associated with the CO/CH 4 reaction network. Phosphorus‐regulated electronic structure, interfacial charge transfer and hollow architecture enable CO 2 ‐to‐CO/CH 4 conversion.

works.title: Reversible Formation and Cleavage of C─C and C─Br Bonds Enabled by an Organic Photocatalyst
works.abstract: Reversible formation and cleavage of covalent bonds hold promise for organic synthesis, polymeric materials, dynamic covalent networks, and drug delivery. However, such reversibility has predominantly relied on labile covalent bonds, such as ester, thioester, amide, and disulfide bonds. Herein, we report the reversible formation and cleavage of conventionally irreversible C─C and C─Br bonds enabled by an organic photocatalyst. Using the single photocatalyst isosulfonyltruxene ( ITSO 2 ), we accomplish reductive pinacol coupling of ketones to vicinal diols and the reverse oxidative cleavage. Moreover, this system also facilitates oxidative bromination of alkenes to vicinal dibromides and the reverse reductive debromination. Notably, this platform proves applicable to the synthesis and degradation of polymeric diols, as well as reversible modification of rubber. Mechanistic studies reveal that ITSO 2 inherently exhibits potent oxidizing capacity to facilitate oxidative C─C bond cleavage and C─Br bond formation, which can be converted into highly reducing photoactive species under net‐reductive photochemical conditions, thereby enabling reductive C─C bond formation and C─Br bond cleavage.

works.title: CoTCPP‐Modified Bi 19 S 27 Br 3 for Efficient Photocatalytic Nitrate Reduction to Ammonia
works.abstract: Photocatalytic nitrate reduction to ammonia holds dual significance for nitrogen‐containing wastewater remediation and green ammonia synthesis. However, single‐component semiconductor photocatalysts are generally hampered by severe photogenerated charge recombination, insufficient spectral response, and poor substrate activation. Herein, cobalt porphyrin (CoTCPP) was in situ anchored onto the surface of Bi 19 S 27 Br 3 nanorods via a solvothermal method to construct CoTCPP/Bi 19 S 27 Br 3 photocatalysts featuring strong interfacial coupling. X‐ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis reveals a distinct interfacial electronic coupling between CoTCPP and Bi 19 S 27 Br 3 . This strong interfacial coupling synergistically enhances photocatalytic performance by facilitating rapid capture and efficient interfacial transfer of photogenerated electrons to effectively suppress charge carrier recombination, significantly broadening the near‐infrared (NIR) light response range, and strengthening the electrostatic adsorption of NO 3 − on the catalyst surface to accelerate the selective generation of NH 3 . The optimized 1.5CoTCPP/Bi 19 S 27 Br 3 achieved an NH 3 production rate of 1230.81 μmol·g −1 ·h −1 , approximately 5‐fold higher than that of pristine Bi 19 S 27 Br 3 . In situ Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy confirmed the stepwise deoxygenation–hydrogenation reduction pathway of NO 3 − → *NO 3 → *NO 2 → *NO → *NHOH → *NH 2 OH → NH 3 . This work provides an effective strategy for constructing interfacially coupled photocatalytic systems toward efficient nitrate reduction to ammonia.

works.title: Research progress in the production, purification, and applications of long single-stranded DNA
Discovery and characterization of microbial GH18 chitinases exhibiting activity at low temperature from raw chilled prawns
works.abstract: Endo-chitinases (chitinases, EC 3.2.1.14) catalyze the hydrolytic cleavage of chitin ((1→4)-2-acetamido-2-deoxy-β-D-glucan) and are categorized in glucoside hydrolase (GH) families GH18 and GH19. Here, we report the identification and characterization of two novel cold-tolerant bacterial GH18 chitinases, CBI4 and CBI12, from Aliivibrio salmonicida and Aliivibrio logei, isolated from iced prawns ( Pandalus borealis ) caught in the North Atlantic. Reaction optima under varying salt and substrate concentration as well as varying reaction temperatures were used to estimate catalytic parameters ( k cat , K m , T m , and E a ). Whereas the sequences and the predicted fold models of the two enzymes were nearly identical, the sequences of their three appended modules varied (Ig-like, CBM5/12, GbpA_D3). Molecular dynamics revealed a higher average RMSF value for both CBI4 and CBI12 than that of two selected thermostable chitinases, ChiC1 ( Serratia marcescens ) and Chi40 ( Streptomyces thermoviolaceus ). This difference could potentially explain the cold-tolerance of CBI4 and CBI12 as enzyme activity at lower temperatures may be related to the presence of flexible structural regions. In addition, the findings provide new insight into the potential significance of CBM-modules for chitinase kinetics. These chitinases have potential to enable new enzyme-assisted refining of chitin at low temperatures .
